So, I have a bit written here. Moments jam up against each other. Staring from a train hurtling through the city, the world flashes by. A mangled jumble of screen impressions seen and not seen, racing forward in a distraction of thoughts, thrown out by cloud-computed algorithms. We're making a new digital world for ourselves. Gone is our leisurely pace of thought and lifestyle. And driven by frictionless connectivity, this digital life is a headlong rush. These photos are an expression of the speed, the cascade of experiences that are the defining aspect of this brave new world. And while my work is, on the one hand, an exploration of how this digital world feels to me, I'm also interested in the question of how the algorithmic devices we populate our lives with experience this very same environment. In other words, how would an AI see the world? The Clipping Suburbia series is generative at its core. The content of the images are compiled entirely by the algorithmic processes of my iPhone's AI as it struggles to cope with the novel experience of recording a panorama from a train window speeding through the landscape at 40 to 50 miles per hour. But, in this struggle, it creates these wonderful images of time and space compressed, of fragments flowing together to form digitized impressions of the world racing by. But, in the end, these results still pose a question. And that is, will AIs see in the same beautifully formed, 3D technicolor renderings as we do, or… Could their world maybe actually be more like this, a constellation of fragmentary images? Or even, perhaps they see something unseeable to us, something entirely of their own imagining. The two worlds, digital space and our experiences of tangible world, are not separate. As we continue incorporating artificial intelligence into our daily lives, we merge. We increasingly experience our world through their eyes, through their senses. And that, I feel, is one of the most important points of this work. For me, especially these smaller images, really feel like the world these days. It feels like everything is rushing too fast. Before you get one thought, another thought comes intruding upon it.
